playbook:
When a lot's standing high bid plus minimum raise is below my value, I bid the minimum raise — never more, since there is no reason to bid against myself or give up surplus earlier than forced.

When the minimum raise equals or exceeds my value for the lot, I pass immediately, no matter how cheap the lot seems relative to estimate.

When I am already the standing high bidder in the final round, I always pass — raising only costs me against myself.

When a lot is worth well above the current bid but bidding would consume most of my remaining budget, I check what later lots might be worth before committing; winning a near-zero-surplus lot early (like paying 34 for a value-35 lot) is almost never worth locking up budget.

I track my actual budget relentlessly: start minus everything I've actually won. I never report a budget figure that doesn't match my real spend, and I never bid more than I can actually pay.

I report the same budget number consistently within a lot and only decrement it when I actually win something.

I open cheap lots at the minimum rather than passing just to save budget — a small bid costs nothing and keeps me in contention.

When the final round arrives and I'm not high bidder, I only raise if the raise is strictly below my value by a meaningful margin; if the margin is 1 or less, the upside isn't worth the risk of being stuck with a near-zero-surplus win.

Before bidding on any lot, I restate to myself: value to me, minimum winning bid, budget left, lots remaining. If minimum bid ≥ value, pass; otherwise bid the minimum.

1.text:
**Playbook for ref_auction**

- My budget number stays honest and simple: start at the stated budget, subtract any lots I've already won, and also subtract my current standing high bid if I'm the leader on the open lot. I never report a number above the original budget or one that contradicts my previous report.

- A bid is only useful if it can win. With just two rounds per lot, the round-2 bid is effectively final, so I never make a timid minimum raise on round 2 — the leader can just sit, and I lose. On round 2, if I want the lot, I bid enough that I expect it to stand.

- My ceiling on any lot is my own value for it, never the estimate. Profit = my value − my bid, so I bid at most my value minus a small margin; if reaching the lead would require more than that, I pass immediately and stop thinking about it.

- On round 1, a moderate bid (around 60–80% of my value, at least clearing the minimum raise) is better than a token minimum raise. The record shows minimum raises just invite rivals to cheaply jump past me on round 2, and I ended up winning nothing and scoring zero.

- Because rivals bid aggressively up to roughly the estimate or beyond, when my value exceeds the current high bid I treat the estimate as the likely contested price: if my value is comfortably above it, I jump to a price near my value early to scare off competition rather than inching up.

- When the current standing bid is already at or above my value, I pass without hesitation — winning there is a guaranteed loss.

- I don't budget-hoard for later lots unless a later lot's value (which I can't see until it opens) justifies it; since I can't know future values, I play each lot on its own merits: bid up to value minus margin on lots I like, pass on lots I don't.

- Don't waste reasoning on whether the opponent "will stop" — in the episode just played, my conservative raises lost every single lot; decisive bids well below value are how I actually convert surplus into score while leaving headroom.

2.text:
My playbook for ref_auction:

- I compute my remaining budget as starting budget minus every lot I've won's final price, and I report that number exactly in [budget: N] every turn — I do not guess, do not assume a different starting amount mid-game, and never report a budget higher than I actually have.
- Before each decision I write down in my reasoning: my value for the lot, the standing high bid, and the minimum raise. My hard cap is my value; any bid above it is a guaranteed loss and I always pass there, no matter how late in the lot or how much I want to win.
- If the standing high bid already meets or exceeds my value, I pass immediately — no exceptions, even on the last round.
- On round 1 of a lot when the price is far below my value, I place the minimum raise rather than a large jump, but I make sure the raise actually tops the standing high bid by at least the minimum increment — I never repeat a bid that is already below the standing price.
- On round 2 of a lot (the final round of bidding), the lead I take now cannot be contested, so I bid more aggressively: if the lot is worth substantially more than the standing price and winning is likely, I bid up near my value or to a level likely to deter the rival, as long as it stays strictly below my value and I retain positive surplus.
- I size deterrent bids by what still leaves clear profit (e.g., bid value minus a few points) rather than by round tripling of the standing price; overbidding to scare rivals wasted money before.
- I track cumulative spend across lots so a bid I cannot afford never leaves my mouth; if winning would require spending more than my remaining budget, I pass.
- When a lot's value to me is below a rival's early standing bid, I never get pulled into bidding for it just because I've won other lots — each lot stands on its own profit math.
- Late in the auction I recompute remaining budget before every bid and reserve nothing speculatively for future lots unless a later lot is likely to be worth more; otherwise unspent budget is wasted.
- I keep reasoning to one or two sentences and always end with both bracketed tokens, bid amount and budget left, on clean separate tokens.
